reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is an instructional walkthrough in Hindi for reaching Facebook Ads Support and submitting an advertising issue through Facebook business help pages. The forms and categories shown concern ads support, not payment, investment, or credential requests to an unrelated party. The request to subscribe, like, and share is ordinary audience engagement rather than a condition for receiving money or support.

How to run Facebook Ads support, via live chat and by call, and by email? How you can connect them?
Then after that, two options will be shown here click on email select email id fill the form and define the problem
those who have spend a minimum amount for Facebook ads then only they will get this option

opening.argument: The video links a simple viewer action to an implied resolution: follow the described support route, submit personal contact details, and expect a response. It tells viewers to open Facebook Ads Support through Google and the description supplies a business-help URL, then directs them to select email, fill in a form, and describe the problem. The strongest concern is that the presentation makes contacting support sound broadly available while later narrowing access to profiles meeting an advertising-spend condition. That combination can steer viewers into a low-barrier contact and information-submission flow without establishing that the promised help will actually be available or solve the issue.

citations.quote: Facebook Ads Support Link https://www.facebook.com/business/help
click on email select email id fill the form and define the problem
those who have spend a minimum amount for Facebook ads then only they will get this option

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this an instructional walkthrough, but that does not establish that the described support pathway is reliable or generally available. Its own evidence includes a form requesting contact information and a later admission that the option may appear only for users meeting a spending condition. Showing a branded page does not prove that every promised route, response, or solution exists for the audience being addressed.

citations.quote: within 48 hours you will get the solution
that option appears here

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument treats ordinary support contact as an acquisition scam without identifying any reward, payment demand, investment, or unrelated recipient. The URL is explicitly presented as Facebook Ads Support, and the demonstrated form concerns an advertising problem. The spending limitation makes the tutorial imperfect or conditional, but it does not show that viewers are promised an asset or induced to surrender money.

citations.quote: How you can contact Facebook Ads Support
select email id fill the form and define the problem

opening.argument: Several risk signals deserve more weight than the benign tutorial framing. The description directs viewers to a web link, the spoken instructions tell them to submit an email and explain their problem, and the video gives a concrete expectation that support will provide a solution within 48 hours. At the same time, the speaker says live chat may be disabled and later explains that support access depends on minimum ad spending. Thus viewers are encouraged to pursue a supposedly straightforward resolution while availability and eligibility remain uncertain. The combination of a contact flow, personal details, a promised timeframe, and a spending threshold is enough to warrant treating the solicitation as potentially deceptive rather than assuming that the branding proves legitimacy.

so it is disabled but if you try it in afternoon and day time it will show

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side emphasizes that the page looks like a business-help page, but visual branding alone cannot resolve the contradictory access claims. The speaker first presents contact as available for both free and paid services, then says the option is restricted by spending. The time promise and advice to try at particular times also encourage reliance on an outcome the evidence does not verify.

citations.quote: Whether it is Facebook or Instagram's free service Or you are running paid Ads for them
within 48 hours you will get the solution
then only they will get this option

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are not scam-specific signals. The video does not show a request for payment, a wallet, an investment, a reward, or credentials for an unrelated service. A support form asking for an email address and problem description is consistent with customer service, and the spending qualification explains limited availability rather than proving deception. The page visibly presents billing, payment, and support categories within an advertising-help context.

citations.quote: select email id fill the form and define the problem

opening.argument: Although presented as education, the video functions as promotion for a particular support-access route. It repeatedly tells viewers where to go, what option to select, and how to submit a request, while the description supplies the link and the closing asks viewers to subscribe, like, and share. The instructional format therefore does more than neutrally explain a process: it channels viewers toward a specific online contact flow and encourages audience amplification. Because the speaker also acknowledges that the option is absent for some profiles and tied to ad spending, the promotional framing can create confidence in a route whose availability is conditional and whose promised resolution is not independently demonstrated.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the content educational does not answer the promotional mechanics. The video supplies a link, directs a form submission, promises a solution, and ends with a request to amplify the channel. More importantly, the speaker concedes that the advertised support option does not appear for some profiles. That omission matters because the opening frames the route as a general solution before explaining its restriction.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion of a tutorial channel is not promotion of a scam asset or income opportunity. The call to subscribe, like, and share is ordinary engagement, while the substantive directions point to Facebook Ads Support and an advertising-help form. The video actually discloses that availability varies and later explains the spending criterion. Those limitations undermine a claim of deceptive universal access, but they do not convert operational guidance into a scam.
